newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Moody's says S.African banks face transition risks.
newsitem.headline: Moody's says S.African banks face transition risks.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on Wednesday that South African banking system was in good condition in the current market context, but cautioned they faced potential credit risks from the larger economic and political transition.
Moody's maintained bank deposit ratings on five of South Africa's largest banks, all of them at Ba1/Not Prime, Moody's highest speculative-grade rating category, it said.

Moody's stressed that the banks' deposit ratings are constrained by the nation's Ba1/Not Prime sovereign ceiling for bank deposits, noting that all of the banks have been assigned relatively high ratings for their inherent, or "stand-alone" financial strength, it added.
Three banks -- First National Bank of Southern Africa, Nedcor Bank Ltd, and Standard Bank of South Africa -- had financial strength ratings of C, indicating good inherent financial strength, it said.
ABSA bank Ltd and NBS Bank Ltd were rated a notch lower at D-Plus, the upper end of the adequate financial strength rating category. it said.

The financial status of each bank was bolstered by its substantial share of the South Africa banking sector, Moody's said, adding that the banks were well developed organisationally, technologically advanced and possess sophicated service offereings.

Moody's said it was likely that the banks would receive timely government assistance, if necessary, despite the fact the officially the South African Reserve bank had adopted a non-interventionist approach to the market.
But it warned the increase in consumer installment lending over the last two years, in combination with more recent rises in interest rates, would lead to higher loan loss rates for the banks.

South Africa's ongoing transtion from apartheid to democratisation would generate the main challenges and risks to the banks' credit quality over the next several years, and high unemployment, currently running above 30 percent and large income disparities remained serious problems that potentially could have broader economic and political implications, it said.
